lines: Morgan Kim
+1 (555) 010-8173 | morgan.kim@example.com | example.com/code/mkim
EDUCATION
Clearwater Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2017 - May 2021
EXPERIENCE
Clearwater Sensors | Hardware Test Engineer | Metro City, USA | Apr 2022 - Feb 2023
- Automated end-of-line tests for a humidity sensor, cutting test time per unit from 90 to 25 seconds across 20,000 units a month.
- Traced a batch of early field failures to a solder-paste change; the findings updated the reflow profile and cut returns from 2.1% to 0.4%.
- Wrote the calibration procedure for the sensor line, cutting calibration drift complaints from 15 to 2 a quarter.
- Designed a test fixture that checked 8 boards at once, raising station throughput from 40 to 150 boards an hour.
Voltline Robotics | Embedded Software Engineer | Metro City, USA | Mar 2023 - Jun 2025
- Improved update speed by 60% by compressing firmware images and resuming interrupted downloads.
- Wrote a hardware-in-the-loop test rig that ran 400 motor-control tests on every firmware build.
- Added a crash logger that saved the last 2 seconds of sensor data to flash, which found the root cause of 5 field failures.
- Sampled the motor's 5 kHz vibration signal at 8 kHz so the fault detector could capture it without aliasing.
- Fixed a race condition on the counter shared by the interrupt handler and the main loop by declaring the counter volatile.
- Rewrote the motor-controller firmware for a warehouse robot fleet of 300 units, cutting control-loop jitter from 120 to 15 microseconds and field motor faults by 60%.
PROJECTS
Low-Power Weather Station | Independent Project | C, STM32 | Jan 2025 - Present
- Engineered a next-generation, innovation-driven IoT solution that redefines sustainable environmental sensing.
- Cut average current from 4.2 mA to 0.9 mA by sleeping between readings and batching radio transmissions.
- Published the schematics and firmware openly, and a local school built two stations from them.
Formula Student Electric Car | Electronics Lead, Team of 12 | C | Sep 2019 - May 2021
- Worked on firmware and testing for the robot fleet's motor controllers.
- The CAN-bus firmware for the dashboard was written and tested against the motor controller before each race.
- Rewrote motor-control firmware for a fleet of about 300 robots, cutting control-loop jitter eightfold and motor faults by more than half.
SKILLS
Tools: C, C++, STM32, oscilloscopes
Methods: firmware, hardware-in-the-loop testing, CAN, low-power design

items.says: The experience entries are not in reverse chronological order.
items.because: Clearwater Sensors appears above the more recent Voltline Robotics role, hiding the career progression.

items.says: The résumé leads with education instead of recent professional experience.
items.because: The embedded-software trajectory is stronger evidence than the degree and should appear sooner.

items.says: The résumé leaves an unexplained 10-month interval between the degree and the first listed role.
items.because: A reader may wonder whether relevant activity is missing from the chronology.

items.says: “Automated end-of-line tests” does not show how the automation was implemented.
“The findings updated the reflow profile” assigns the update to the findings rather than a person or process.
items.because: Findings can prompt an update but cannot perform one, making the causal chain unclear.

items.says: “Traced a batch of early field failures” does not show how the diagnosis was reached.
The strongest Clearwater Sensors bullet is not placed first.
“Wrote the calibration procedure” does not show its technically important content.
The test-fixture bullet gives capacity without identifying the mechanism that enabled it.
“Improved update speed by 60%” does not identify the metric or comparison points.
items.because: A reader cannot tell whether the figure concerns download duration, transfer throughput, or installation time.

items.says: “Improved update speed by 60% by” repeats “by” awkwardly.
The test-rig bullet gives test volume but no resulting improvement.
“Which found the root cause” ambiguously suggests that the logger or flash storage performed the analysis.
Sampling a 5 kHz signal at 8 kHz cannot capture that component without aliasing.
items.because: An 8 kHz sample rate has a 4 kHz Nyquist frequency, below the stated signal frequency.

items.says: The bullet states an intended fault-detection capability rather than a demonstrated result.
Declaring the shared counter volatile does not fix a race condition.
items.because: Volatile provides neither atomicity nor synchronization between the interrupt handler and main loop.

items.says: “Fixed a race condition” does not identify the observable failure or result of the fix.
The 300-unit firmware-rewrite accomplishment is assigned to both Voltline Robotics and Formula Student.
items.because: The Formula Student entry repeats the apparent work and results, creating a credibility problem.

items.says: The jitter and fault reductions are buried after the method and fleet scope.
items.because: Leading with the results would show the impact sooner.

items.says: “Rewrote the motor-controller firmware” does not identify the engineering decision that produced the results.
The strongest Voltline Robotics bullet is not placed first.
“Next-generation, innovation-driven IoT solution” is promotional filler that does not identify the station’s function or technical approach.
items.because: A technical reader cannot tell what engineering work or embedded-system skill it demonstrates.

items.says: “Redefines sustainable environmental sensing” claims a change without identifying the change or supporting evidence.
items.because: A reader cannot distinguish a meaningful result from promotional language.

items.says: The strongest weather-station bullet is not placed first.
The average-current figures omit the sampling and transmission conditions under which they were measured.
items.because: Reading and transmission frequency affect average current, so the figures may not be comparable.

items.says: “Published the schematics and firmware openly” does not say where they are available.
“The robot fleet’s motor controllers” is wrongly placed in a Formula Student electric-car project.
items.because: Formula Student work concerns the competition car, not a robot fleet.

items.says: “Worked on firmware and testing” does not identify the actions, firmware changed, or testing performed.
items.because: The wording obscures personal ownership and what embedded engineering was done.

items.says: The motor-controller bullet gives no result.
items.because: It does not show what the work improved, verified, or enabled.

items.says: The broad motor-controller bullet repeats the more specific robot-fleet accomplishment later in the entry.
items.because: The later line includes the scale and outcomes, so the vague version adds repetition rather than evidence.

items.says: “CAN-bus” is not the standard spelling of the technology name.
items.because: The standard term is “CAN bus,” without a hyphen.

items.says: The passive voice in “was written and tested” hides the candidate’s actions.
items.because: An active opening would show ownership of the writing and testing.

items.says: “Before each race” says when testing occurred but not what it achieved.
The CAN-dashboard bullet is not placed first despite being the strongest line clearly belonging to Formula Student.
“Tested against the motor controller” does not explain which behavior or interface was validated.
The claim about a fleet of about 300 robots is wrongly attributed to Formula Student.
items.because: Formula Student develops a competition vehicle, and the line mirrors the Voltline accomplishment.

items.says: “Rewrote motor-control firmware” does not identify the technical mechanism behind the reported improvements.
items.because: Without the timing, scheduling, concurrency, or control change, the results cannot be evaluated technically.
